steps.title: What makes an autopsy medicolegal
steps.tx: A **medicolegal autopsy** is performed on the order of an investigating authority in unnatural, sudden or suspicious death, and it aims to establish identity, cause of death, time since death and the nature of any injuries. Unlike a clinical autopsy, it needs no consent from relatives, but it demands a complete external and internal examination with photography and preserved samples. Every finding may later be tested in court.
steps.say: A medicolegal autopsy answers identity, cause, timing and injuries for the law, and needs authority, not family consent.

steps.title: Virchow technique, organ by organ
steps.tx: In the **Virchow technique**, organs are removed and dissected one by one: cranial cavity first, then thoracic, cervical and abdominal organs in turn, with the spinal cord taken from the back. The method suits focused examination of a single diseased organ. Its price is that anatomical relations between organs are lost as each organ leaves the body, so connections such as a fistula or an embolus path can be missed.
steps.say: Virchow removes organs one at a time, which is tidy for single organs but breaks the relations between them.

nodes.label: Dissect each organ on the board

steps.title: Rokitansky technique and infective cases
steps.tx: The **Rokitansky technique** combines in situ dissection with removal of organs in blocks, keeping much of the dissection inside the body. Reddy names it the preferred choice when the dead person carried a highly transmissible disease such as HIV or hepatitis B, because fewer free organs are handled on the open board. The pathologist still inspects each system in place before any block is lifted out.
steps.say: Rokitansky dissects largely in place, and that contained approach is preferred for HIV or hepatitis B bodies.

steps.title: Letulle en masse removal
steps.tx: The **Letulle technique** removes the cervical, thoracic, abdominal and pelvic organs together as one mass, tongue to rectum, and dissects that block outside the body. Every attachment stays intact, so the aorta, oesophagus, trachea and bowel can be followed without a single cut across their connections. Reddy describes freeing the neck structures, diaphragm and pelvic floor so the whole block pulls forward and out in one piece.
steps.say: Letulle lifts tongue to rectum out as one block, keeping every connection intact for the board dissection.

steps.title: Ghon en bloc removal by systems
steps.tx: The **Ghon technique** is the middle path: cervical, thoracic and abdominal organs come out as separate system blocks, and the urogenital system forms another block of its own. Relations survive inside each block while the blocks stay small enough to handle and photograph cleanly. Many teaching mortuaries default to Ghon for routine medicolegal work because it balances anatomical continuity against a manageable dissection field.
steps.say: Ghon removes organs in system blocks, a compromise that keeps local relations without one unwieldy mass.

steps.title: Exhumation needs a Magistrate order
steps.tx: **Exhumation** is the lawful digging out of an already buried body, and in India there is no time limit for ordering it. It serves criminal cases such as disguised homicide, suspected poisoning and criminal negligence, plus civil claims over insurance, compensation and disputed identity. The body is exhumed only on the written order of an Executive Magistrate, under a medical officer, in the presence of police, preferably in natural light.
steps.say: India sets no time limit on exhumation, but a written Executive Magistrate order and daylight digging are mandatory.

nodes.label: Grave identified by plot and marker

steps.title: Conduct of the exhumation
steps.tx: The team uncovers the grave ten to fifteen centimetres at a time, notes soil, water and plant growth, and measures depth to skull and feet in a careful **exhumation procedure**. The body is brushed clean, photographed where it lies and lifted on a plank or sheet. In suspected mineral poisoning, about half a kilogram of earth in contact with the body, plus samples from above, below and each side, goes for analysis with a piece of coffin and clothing.
steps.say: Dig in shallow layers, photograph before lifting, and send contact soil for analysis whenever mineral poisoning is alleged.

steps.title: Second autopsy and its limits
steps.tx: A **second autopsy** on an exhumed, previously autopsied body is difficult because decay merges contusions, blurs patterns and the first dissection has already altered the anatomy. Before starting, gather the first report, scene and autopsy photographs, hospital records and X rays, and invite the first pathologist if possible. Contusions can paradoxically become visible once blood drains from tissues after the first autopsy, so detailed documentation still has value.
steps.say: A second autopsy fights decay and prior cuts, yet drained tissues sometimes reveal contusions the first examination missed.

steps.title: When the autopsy finds nothing, first thoughts
steps.tx: Occasionally the full examination ends without a cause, the seed of the **negative autopsy** discussed in the next lesson. Inadequate history heads the causes: vagal inhibition, status epilepticus and hypersensitivity can kill without leaving anatomical findings. Missed needle marks, snake bite punctures and small electric burns punish a cursory external examination. The honest response is more history, more laboratory work and re-examination, not a guessed cause.
steps.say: A blank autopsy usually means missing history or a missed surface mark, so look again before concluding anything.
